section: §4.2 Prilocaine, and the lidocaine–prilocaine cream (EMLA) › 4.2.1 The evidence in neuropathic pain
sentence_as_it_stands: **Eleven more, also post-herpetic, are the only people anywhere given repeated daily EMLA in an established neuropathic pain state** — **[dose figure omitted]**. … **That is the one EMLA dataset describing the regimen this reference is evaluating, and its responder predictor is the one §9.3 is built around — preserved thermal function.**
quote: This clinical trial was designed to compare the safety and efficacy of daily application of the EMLA cream ... After 4 weeks of treatment, patients in both groups reported significant changes (P < 0.001) in pain intensity.
corrected_wording: Eleven more, also post-herpetic, are the only patients with postherpetic neuralgia given repeated daily EMLA with quantitative sensory testing (Attal 1999), and their responder predictor is the one §9.3 is built around — preserved thermal function. Daily application of the cream has also been studied for four weeks in carpal tunnel syndrome, in a randomised open-label trial against a steroid injection in which pain fell in both arms (Moghtaderi 2009).
notes: Same error as claim D066 (refuted), recorded as a further place it appears. Deciding source Moghtaderi 2009 (PMID 19845100), taken from the D066 claim record, not from Effendy's reference list; abstract cached. Effendy 2015 is not a counter-example: no patient was described as neuropathic. The §4.2 evidence line just above ('Evidence SERIES (n=12) + SERIES (n=11) + 2 CASES, all uncontrolled — plus one randomised placebo-controlled trial, n=46, which tested prevention and not treatment') omits the same trial.

page: 2 — Reference — Topical Treatments for Small Fiber Neuropathy
section: §4.2 Prilocaine, and the lidocaine–prilocaine cream (EMLA) › 4.2.1 The evidence in neuropathic pain
sentence_as_it_stands: **The extensive remainder of the EMLA literature is procedural anaesthesia, which is a different question again.**
quote: We report a study designed to determine the plasma concentrations of lidocaine and prilocaine during repeated daily application, for 10 days, of [dose figure omitted] EMLA to leg ulcers, and to evaluate the analgesic effect on chronic ulcer pain.
corrected_wording: Most of the remaining EMLA literature is procedural anaesthesia, which is a different question again. A small part studies the cream in chronic leg-ulcer pain: daily application before debridement for ten days, with chronic ulcer pain and plasma levels followed (Effendy 2015, open, uncontrolled), and daily use as a wound dressing for four weeks (Purcell 2017, pilot randomised trial). That is wound pain, not neuropathic pain.
notes: Ambiguous rather than plainly wrong (brief section 6): as a description of the bulk of the literature the sentence is accurate; read as exhaustive it misses a small chronic wound-pain literature — Effendy 2015 (outcome: daily pre-application rating of chronic ulcer pain over ten days), Purcell 2017 (PMID 28727591, from Effendy's reference 13 and a PubMed search) and Stymne 2001 (already the Reference's S58). None of it bears on neuropathic efficacy.

section: Sources › S451 (EMLA in neuropathic pain — the whole of it, and the one randomised trial in it)
sentence_as_it_stands: Attal 1999 is the only test of a **repeated daily** regimen anywhere in this literature, and it has 11 patients. **Nothing in the set measures a nerve fibre, and nothing in it runs beyond six days.**
quote: This clinical trial was designed to compare the safety and efficacy of daily application of the EMLA cream ... After 4 weeks of treatment, patients in both groups reported significant changes (P < 0.001) in pain intensity.
corrected_wording: Attal 1999 is the only repeated daily regimen among these reports used to treat an established pain state, and it has 11 patients (Fassoulaki 2000 applied the cream daily in the days after surgery, as prevention); nothing in the set measures a nerve fibre, and nothing in it runs beyond six days. Outside the set, daily application has been studied for four weeks in carpal tunnel syndrome, in a randomised open-label trial against a steroid injection (Moghtaderi 2009).
notes: Same error as claim D066, a further place it appears. 'This literature' is S451's 'EMLA in neuropathic pain — the whole of it', so Moghtaderi 2009 (PMID 19845100, from the D066 claim record, not Effendy's reference list) falls inside it. The S451 title's 'the one randomised trial in it' is the D067 question (Flondell 2017/2024, Fassoulaki 2005), left to S-686-43's session. Effendy 2015 is not neuropathic and is not a counter-example. Within S451 itself, the Fassoulaki 2000 entry describes daily application in the days after surgery, so even inside the set 'the only test of a repeated daily regimen' needs the qualifier 'to treat an established pain state'.

section: Sources › The Reynolds series — St Thomas' Hospital, 1976 to 1985 (Aps C, Reynolds F 1976 entry); also the Reynolds-series table cell 'Primary numbers not read. Known only second-hand'
sentence_as_it_stands: **Limits: primary numbers not read.** No abstract is indexed and the full text is not available through any route tried here; everything above is second-hand from the group's own later papers. The sample size of 31 comes from a secondary account and was not verified at source. quote: In a double-blind trial bupivacaine [dose figure omitted] and lignocaine [dose figure omitted] were given intradermally to 31 volunteers. Vasoconstriction was observed more frequently at low concentrations of each drug, and vasodilatation at high concentrations. ... Duration of action was unaffected by concentration, except in the case of bupivacaine [dose figure omitted], the effect of which was longer lasting than that of other solutions.
corrected_wording: **Limits:** PubMed indexes an abstract (PMID 1023952). It confirms a double-blind intradermal trial in 31 volunteers, with vasoconstriction more frequent at low and vasodilatation at high concentrations of each drug (P < 0.001), and duration unaffected by concentration except at the highest bupivacaine strength, which lasted longer. The abstract does make that exception; the 1985 summary, which compares only the two lower strengths, does not mention it. The primary duration figures are still unread.
